articles.title: Singapore's ultraviolet day, hour by hour
articles.standfirst: Singapore lies roughly one and a half degrees north of the equator, its day length varies by about an hour across the entire year16, and the National Environment Agency reports that it is common for the ultraviolet index to reach Very High and Extreme levels in the four-hour period between 11am and 3pm on a day with little cloud cover8. Yet fewer than a quarter of adults surveyed here apply sunscreen2. This article sets out what is measured, when, and what follows from it for skin.
articles.sub: What the national measurements show about when the sun here is actually dangerous, and what that means for skin at this latitude.

blocks.html: What the ultraviolet index measures

The ultraviolet index is a standardised scale developed jointly by the World Health Organization, the United Nations Environment Programme and the World Meteorological Organization to express the intensity of ultraviolet radiation at ground level8. The scale is weighted for erythema, calibrated to the wavelengths that redden human skin rather than to total ultraviolet energy.

The index is measured here with a sensor sited in an open field at the Changi Meteorological Station, and reported every fifteen minutes between 7am and 7pm, each value representing the average of the preceding fifteen minutes78. The scale runs from 0 to 11 and above, grouped into five categories. Readings above 11 are considered Extreme, and those between 8 and 10 Very High1. World Health Organization guidance attaches protective behaviour to those categories: at 3 to 7, seek shade during midday hours and use a shirt, sunscreen and hat; at 8 and above, avoid being outside during midday hours altogether14.
“A high UV Index reading means a larger dose of UV radiation for the same amount of time spent in the sun.”

What the sky here delivers on an ordinary day

The Meteorological Service Singapore gives the typical daily maximum ultraviolet index as six to nine1, which places an ordinary cloudless afternoon in the High to Very High categories before any unusual conditions are involved. In every month the protective threshold of 3 is routinely exceeded around the middle of the day.

What varies through the year is not solar geometry but the atmosphere in front of it. Day length runs to roughly twelve hours and differs by about an hour between the longest and shortest days16, and the sun is close to overhead in every month. Annual variation is therefore driven mainly by cloud, with the highest values occurring in months with less of it: February, March, April and September tend to see the highest ultraviolet radiation1.

The National Environment Agency publishes its hourly index readings as an open dataset. The 2024 record alone contains more than 32,000 hourly observations from the Changi station6, which is the resource anyone wanting to characterise the local ultraviolet day in detail should be working from.
One measured afternoon, hour by hour

The clearest way to see the shape of the day is to follow a single one. On 27 March 2024 the index at Changi first entered the Extreme band at about 12.15pm with a reading of 11. It climbed to 12 at about 1.15pm. By 2.45pm it had fallen back to 101.

Three points, roughly two and a half hours apart, describe the whole problem. The reading was already in the highest category before the lunch hour was over, it peaked in the early afternoon rather than at midday, and it was still Very High at a quarter to three. An office worker leaving the building at 12.30pm and returning at 2pm was outdoors for the entire span.

Why the clock misleads you

Singapore keeps time eight hours ahead of Coordinated Universal Time, but sits at a longitude nearer to seven. The consequence is that solar noon, the moment the sun reaches its highest point, falls at around 1pm rather than at midday: in January it occurs at approximately 1.13pm, with sunrise at 7.11am and sunset at 7.16pm16.

This is why the 27 March peak arrived when it did. The four-hour window of highest intensity is not symmetrical around twelve o'clock, and the intuition that danger peaks at lunchtime and recedes through the early afternoon is displaced by roughly an hour. The 11am to 3pm window published by the National Environment Agency8 accommodates this, but the underlying reason is rarely explained, and a 2.30pm walk is frequently treated as safer than it is.
What reaches the skin

Terrestrial ultraviolet radiation is conventionally divided into ultraviolet B, spanning approximately 290 to 320 nanometres, and ultraviolet A, spanning 320 to 400 nanometres3. The proportions are heavily skewed. Ultraviolet B accounts for around 0.5 per cent of solar spectral irradiance at ground level, while ultraviolet A represents approximately 95 per cent of the ultraviolet radiation reaching the surface and is at least twenty times more abundant315.

The two behave differently in tissue. Of the ultraviolet B reaching the skin, around 70 per cent is absorbed by the stratum corneum, 20 per cent reaches the viable epidermis and only 10 per cent penetrates the upper dermis. Ultraviolet A travels further, with 20 to 30 per cent reaching the deep dermis. Ultraviolet B is the more effective waveband for producing erythema by roughly three orders of magnitude, which is why the index is weighted towards it; ultraviolet A appears to play the major role in the deterioration of dermal structure that produces the photoaged appearance3.

Sunburn is a signal generated almost entirely by the minority waveband. The waveband responsible for most dermal change produces no immediate sensation at all, is present in far greater quantity throughout the reporting day, and passes through window glass.

What cloud and reflection do and do not change

Cloud cover is the most common source of false reassurance. The World Health Organization states that light or thin cloud has little effect on ultraviolet levels and may even enhance them through scattering15. In a climate with substantial convective cloud but frequent breaks, this produces a pattern in which the index falls sharply during a thunderstorm and returns to Very High shortly afterwards, while the subjective impression is of an overcast day.

Reflected radiation adds to direct exposure and is not blocked by conventional shade. Dry sand reflects approximately 15 per cent of incident ultraviolet radiation and sea foam approximately 25 per cent15. A parasol on a beach, or an umbrella on a bright pavement, reduces the direct component while leaving the scattered and reflected components largely intact.

Shade nonetheless remains the single most effective measure available, and the index-linked guidance is explicit that it should be sought from a value of 3 upwards and that outdoor exposure should be avoided from 814. On an ordinary afternoon sitting between 6 and 91, that is not an occasional instruction.
What this does to skin here, and what people do

The clinical picture at this latitude is dominated by pigment rather than by cancer. Analysis of 12,692 skin cancers recorded by the Singapore Cancer Registry between 1968 and 2016 found melanoma accounted for 5.8 per cent of cases, with melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma incidence remaining low and stable across the Chinese, Malay and Indian populations; basal cell carcinoma was the subtype that rose11. Pigmented changes, meanwhile, constitute the major sign of skin photoageing in Asian populations3, and melasma, the symmetrical facial hyperpigmentation that predominates in Fitzpatrick skin types III and IV, is both common and difficult to treat: a randomised trial conducted at the National Skin Centre required daily SPF 50 or higher in every arm as baseline care4.

Against that, local behaviour is poorly matched to local exposure. A cross-sectional survey of 2,328 adults found that 14.2 per cent wore protective headgear, 18.8 per cent used umbrellas regularly and 23.9 per cent applied a sunscreen of SPF 30 or above. Mean daily sun exposure was 1.45 hours. Just over half the sample, 53.4 per cent, had Fitzpatrick type III skin and a further 19.1 per cent type IV, which is precisely the group in which melasma predominates. Men, those with darker skin types and those with lower education spent more time in the sun and scored lower on protection2.

“Although [having dark skin] can have a certain protective effect, if they do not wear sunscreen and are exposed to the sun for long periods of time, they will have a higher chance of suffering from skin cancer.”
blocks.cite: Dr Yew Yik Weng, National Skin Centre, co-author of the survey12

blocks.html: What adequate protection looks like, and what the evidence supports

Sun protection factor is determined under laboratory conditions at an application density of 2 milligrams per square centimetre5. Application in ordinary use is generally well below that density, and because the relationship between quantity and protection is not linear, the protection achieved is materially lower than the labelled figure. Reapplication through a day of 6 to 9 is what makes the labelled figure approximately true.

The guidance issued locally is for a broad-spectrum product of at least SPF 30, reapplied approximately every two hours, together with umbrellas, broad-brimmed hats and sunglasses1. Ultraviolet A dominates the incident spectrum and passes through glass, so a product's ultraviolet A performance matters as much as its sun protection factor. Where a patient has recently undergone a light or laser procedure, daily photoprotection is recommended from the first day afterwards and maintained for three to six months, with visible-light protection where pigmentary relapse is the concern17.

Formulation choice is also a compliance question. Heat and humidity raise sebum production and sweat rate, and a product that is not tolerable to wear in this climate is not applied, which makes texture a clinical variable rather than a cosmetic preference. Where reapplication over make-up during the working day is the obstacle, powder and stick formats exist precisely to remove it.

The underlying benefit has been tested. A randomised controlled trial assigned 1,621 adults to daily or discretionary sunscreen use and followed them for well over a decade; invasive melanoma occurred in three participants in the daily-use group against eleven in the discretionary group, a hazard ratio of 0.27 with a confidence interval of 0.08 to 0.979. In the same cohort, 903 adults under 55 followed for four and a half years showed 24 per cent less skin ageing on blinded assessment when assigned to daily use10. The most frequently raised objection does not survive examination either: a review of experimental studies, field trials and 69 observational studies concluded that there is little evidence that sunscreen decreases 25-hydroxyvitamin D concentration in real-life settings, although the authors note that the field trials used sunscreen of around SPF 1618.

The index sits in the High to Very High range on an ordinary afternoon, there is no month in which that stops being true, and on 27 March 2024 it was still at 10 at a quarter to three. Protection here is a daily variable, and the four hours between 11am and 3pm are the ones that determine most of the annual dose.

faq.q: What is a normal ultraviolet index for Singapore?
faq.a: The Meteorological Service Singapore gives the typical daily maximum as six to nine, which corresponds to the High and Very High categories. On 27 March 2024 the reading at Changi reached 121. The National Environment Agency reports that Very High and Extreme levels are common between 11am and 3pm on a day with little cloud cover8.

The four hours from 11am to 3pm8. Because Singapore's clock runs about an hour ahead of its solar time, solar noon falls at around 1.13pm rather than at midday16, which is why the peak reading on 27 March 2024 was recorded at about 1.15pm1.
February, March, April and September tend to see the highest ultraviolet radiation, because annual variation here is driven by cloud cover rather than by the sun's elevation1.

faq.q: Does an overcast day mean I can skip sunscreen?
faq.a: No. The World Health Organization states that light or thin cloud has little effect on ultraviolet levels and may even enhance them through scattering15. In a climate of frequent short storms and rapid clearing, the subjective impression of an overcast day is a poor guide to the measured index.

faq.q: Is sunscreen still necessary indoors or in a car?
faq.a: Ultraviolet A accounts for approximately 95 per cent of the ultraviolet radiation reaching ground level315, penetrates to the deep dermis3, and passes through window glass. For anyone managing pigmentation or photoageing, daily use is the relevant standard rather than outdoor use.

articles.title: Sun protection you swallow
articles.standfirst: A capsule that makes your skin harder to burn sounds like the answer to a country where the ultraviolet index sits between six and nine on an ordinary day.1 The version the evidence supports is narrower than the marketing and more interesting than the scepticism. Here is what has been measured in people, who funded the measuring, and where the evidence runs out.
articles.sub: What oral photoprotection can and cannot do, read against the trials rather than the packaging.

blocks.html: What is in the capsule

Oral photoprotection, as sold in Singapore and across Europe, almost always means one ingredient: an extract of Polypodium leucotomos, a fern native to Central America. In the Heliocare range the standardised version of this extract is branded Fernblock, and the manufacturer describes it as working through antioxidant activity, support for the skin's DNA repair processes, and protection of the immune cells in the skin that ultraviolet light suppresses.2

The daily capsule format in the Heliocare 360 range pairs the extract with niacinamide, vitamin E and vitamin D, and is taken once a day before sun exposure.3 Doses across the published research vary considerably by indication, from 240 mg daily up to 1,200 mg, and no standard protocol has been established.4

Extraction method appears to change what the extract does. The authors of the largest photoprotection review state plainly that their findings “cannot be extrapolated to other formulations” of Polypodium leucotomos.5 A generic fern extract bought online is not the same product as a standardised pharmaceutical-grade one, and the research on one does not transfer to the other.
What the trials measured

The most-used endpoint in this literature is the minimal erythema dose, the amount of ultraviolet energy needed to produce a just-visible reddening of the skin. If a supplement raises it, the skin has become measurably harder to burn.

A 2018 systematic review pooled 18 studies of oral Polypodium leucotomos for photoprotection and found that most reported a benefit on this measure, with no serious adverse effects recorded.5 A broader 2025 review identified 21 qualifying studies including 11 randomised controlled trials, spanning photoageing, actinic keratosis, photodermatoses, melasma, vitiligo and atopic dermatitis.4

That sounds substantial until you look at the size of the individual studies. In the 2018 review, sample sizes ranged from five participants to sixty-one.5 These are small, mostly short trials, and several were funded by the manufacturer. The effect appears real and consistent in direction, but not large, and it has not been demonstrated at the scale that would settle the question.
Where the evidence is strongest

The single most convincing study is not about sunburn at all. In a randomised trial across two Italian centres, 131 patients with photodamaged skin and at least three actinic keratoses, which are the rough precancerous patches that develop on chronically sun-exposed skin, were assigned to one of three regimens for twelve months: SPF 100+ sunscreen alone, sunscreen plus a topical Polypodium leucotomos cream, or sunscreen plus both the topical cream and 240 mg of the oral extract daily.6

Of the 116 who completed, disease progressed in 38% of the sunscreen-only group, 11% of the topical group and 2% of the group taking the capsule as well. Severity scores improved by 7% in the extract groups while worsening by 6% in the controls.6

A senior author holds financial relationships with the manufacturer, and the investigators themselves called for larger and adequately powered studies before this changes clinical practice. Separately, a planned independent trial of the extract for skin cancer prevention at Massachusetts General Hospital was withdrawn in 2019 for lack of funding, before a single participant was enrolled.7 The question of whether oral photoprotection prevents skin cancer has not been asked properly yet.
The melasma question, and the Singapore trial

Melasma matters more here than sunburn does: the symmetrical brown patching across the cheeks, forehead and upper lip is common in Fitzpatrick III and IV skin, worsens with sun and heat, and recurs stubbornly.

Singapore has its own trial. At the National Skin Centre, 40 patients with Fitzpatrick III–IV skin were randomised to 480 mg of oral extract twice daily or placebo for twelve weeks, with everyone also using 4% hydroquinone nightly and SPF 50+ daily.8 Among the 33 evaluated, severity scores fell by 54.9% on the extract and 44.4% on placebo. The gap between the two groups was statistically significant at day 56, when the extract group had improved 49.4% against the placebo group's 32.6%.

Patients on the extract improved faster, and by three months both groups had improved substantially. This was a small pilot, it was sponsored by the manufacturer, and two of its authors were employees of that manufacturer.8 The broader 2025 review records melasma results across the literature as mixed, with at least one study finding no significant benefit over placebo.4
On this evidence the capsule is not a melasma treatment. It may be something that gets an existing treatment working sooner.
The line the category is not allowed to cross

In May 2018 the United States Food and Drug Administration issued warning letters to four companies marketing dietary supplements with sun-protection claims: GliSODin Skin Nutrients, Napa Valley Bioscience, Pharmacy Direct and Sunergized.9 The agency's position was that a product claiming to protect against ultraviolet damage is making a drug claim, which requires drug approval.

Heliocare was not among the companies that received those letters. But the episode set the boundary for the whole category, and it is worth knowing where it sits. Dermatologists commenting at the time drew the same distinction that the evidence supports: there is no such thing as an oral sunscreen, and a well-researched extract can still be a reasonable adjunct to photoprotection provided it is not sold as a replacement for it.9

The practical rule

Nothing in the published evidence supports taking a capsule instead of applying sunscreen. Every trial described above gave participants topical sunscreen as well, usually SPF 50+ or SPF 100+. The capsule was always tested as an addition, never as a substitute, so an addition is the only thing it has been shown to be.
The part that is not in doubt
An article on the capsule can easily skip past the evidence for the cream, which is considerably stronger.

In the Nambour trial in Queensland, 1,621 adults were randomised to daily sunscreen or discretionary use and then followed for well over a decade. Invasive melanoma occurred in three participants in the daily-use group against eleven in the discretionary group, a hazard ratio of 0.27 with a confidence interval of 0.08 to 0.97.10 The result for melanoma overall did not quite reach statistical significance, which is worth stating rather than rounding away.

The same cohort produced the strongest photoageing finding available anywhere. Among 903 adults under 55 followed for four and a half years, those assigned to daily sunscreen showed 24% less skin ageing on blinded assessment than those using it at their discretion.11 No supplement has evidence approaching that.

And the most common reason people give for skipping daily application does not hold up. A review of experimental studies, field trials and 69 observational studies concluded that there is “little evidence that sunscreen decreases 25(OH)D concentration when used in real-life settings.”12 The authors do note a genuine gap: the randomised field trials used moderate-protection sunscreen of around SPF 16, and no trial has yet tested the high-SPF products people are now advised to use.
What this means in a country with no low season

Singapore sits close enough to the equator that the sun is near-overhead for most of the year. Daily maximum ultraviolet index readings average six to nine, peaking between 10am and 3pm, and readings of 12 to 15 have been recorded during clear spells.1 The exposure argument never goes quiet here.

The local risk profile is also not the one imported from Britain or Australia. Analysis of 12,692 skin cancers recorded by the Singapore Cancer Registry between 1968 and 2016 found melanoma accounted for 5.8% of cases, with melanoma and squamous cell carcinoma rates remaining low and stable across all three major ethnic groups. Basal cell carcinoma, the least dangerous of the three, was the one that rose.13

What that leaves as the realistic daily concern is pigmentation and photoageing rather than cancer, which is precisely where the sunscreen evidence is strongest and where the oral evidence, such as it is, also sits.
So, is it worth taking?
A defensible reading of the evidence looks something like this.

• It is not a substitute. Nothing in the literature supports replacing topical sunscreen, and every trial included it.
  • It is best supported as an adjunct in specific situations: alongside treatment for melasma, alongside sunscreen in people with significant photodamage or actinic keratoses, and in people whose skin reacts abnormally to sunlight, where the evidence is real but uncontrolled.14
  • The formulation matters and the research does not transfer between different extracts.5
  • The safety record is reassuring across the studies conducted so far, with no serious adverse effects reported.54
  • The trials are small and often sponsor-funded, so the appropriate confidence is moderate rather than high.

If you are choosing between buying the capsule and applying sunscreen properly every morning, the evidence is not close. Apply the sunscreen. If you are already doing that, are being treated for pigmentation or photodamage, and want to add something with a plausible mechanism and a decade of small positive trials behind it, the capsule is a reasonable conversation to have with your dermatologist.
What we still do not know

Three questions remain open. Whether oral photoprotection reduces skin cancer incidence has never been tested in an adequately powered independent trial, and the one attempt was withdrawn before enrolment.7 Optimal dosing has not been established, with published regimens ranging from 240 mg to 1,200 mg daily.4 And the effects on visible light and infrared radiation, which are described mechanistically in the manufacturer's own materials, rest largely on laboratory work rather than the human clinical endpoints that carry the ultraviolet claims.2
Those gaps are not a reason to dismiss the ingredient. They are the reason to describe it accurately, and to keep applying the cream.

articles.title: What the haze is doing to skin
articles.standfirst: At 11am on 9 September 2026 the twenty-four hour Pollutant Standards Index across Singapore's five regions read between 72 and 931. Days earlier it had crossed 100 for the first time since October 20232. The skincare advice circulating in response has been confident and almost entirely unsourced. What the published evidence supports is narrower, and it runs out sooner than the advice does.
articles.sub: Particulate matter is the insult and ultraviolet is the multiplier. Read against the studies, the case for changing anything is narrower than this week's advice suggests.

blocks.html: What is in the air this week

The National Environment Agency attributes this episode to smoke plumes from fires in southern and central Sumatra and parts of Kalimantan, carried over Singapore on southeasterly and southerly winds3. On 4 September the one-hour PM2.5 concentration measured across the island ranged from 41 to 83 micrograms per cubic metre, and the twenty-four hour PSI from 83 to 1163. By 7 September those had eased to 22 to 36 and 63 to 85 respectively, with the agency still forecasting a moderate to low unhealthy range while dry conditions persist4.

For skin the number that matters is not the PSI but PM2.5, the fraction of airborne particulate below 2.5 micrometres in aerodynamic diameter, which the mechanistic literature attributes chiefly to open fires, vehicle exhaust and power generation5 and which in this episode is coming from burning in Sumatra and Kalimantan4. The PSI is a composite across several pollutants, but in a haze episode PM2.5 is the sub-index driving it: in the 9 September reading, the twenty-four hour PSI in all five regions was identical to that region's PM2.5 sub-index1. At 3pm on 8 September the one-hour PM2.5 reading in central Singapore was 58 micrograms per cubic metre6.

The skin evidence is mostly about pigment

The best-known work on particulate matter and skin is not about haze at all, but a follow-up of the German SALIA cohort, in which 400 women aged 70 to 80 were examined against decades of residential exposure to traffic soot and background particulate7. Each increase in soot exposure was associated with roughly 20% more pigment spots on the forehead and cheeks, and each increase in traffic-derived particles with 16 to 17% more7. Nasolabial folds deepened slightly. Wrinkles, notably, showed no significant association anywhere on the face.

A Chinese cohort of 1,877 adults found the same signal indoors: an interquartile rise in modelled indoor PM2.5 was associated with 12.5% more pigment spots on the forehead and 7.7% more upper-lip wrinkling8. Two independent populations and two different exposure routes produced the same finding. That consistency is why the pigmentation claim is the sturdiest thing in this literature.

That sturdiness comes with a limit. Both studies measure exposure accumulated across decades of ordinary urban living, and neither tells you what one week of haze does to a face. Anyone extrapolating from a lifetime of soot to a fortnight of smoke is doing something the data does not license.
The Singapore study, and what it puts a number on

One piece of local evidence speaks directly to short-term exposure. Researchers at the National Skin Centre analysed 1,440,844 atopic dermatitis consultations recorded between 2009 and 2019 against daily air quality, using distributed lag models out to six weeks9. At the 90th percentile of PM2.5, 24.4 micrograms per cubic metre, the risk of an eczema consultation was 10% higher than at the median of 16.1, with a confidence interval of 1.01 to 1.199. At the 10th percentile it was 14% lower. Nitrogen dioxide, sulphur dioxide, ozone and carbon monoxide showed no significant association at all.

The finding is more modest than it first sounds. The eleven years it covers include the 2013 and 2015 haze episodes, so bad air days are inside the range it modelled rather than outside it. The effect is real, specific to a defined inflammatory condition rather than to skin in general, and amounts to a 10% shift in consultations rather than a transformation. The study establishes that when the particulate load in Singapore rises, more people come in with eczema. That is locally measured, and it is the whole of what has been shown.

On comparing this week's numbers to the study

Setting the 58 micrograms per cubic metre recorded in central Singapore on 8 September6 against the study's 90th percentile of 24.49 makes it look as though the risk has more than doubled. That comparison does not hold. The first is a one-hour reading and the second a twenty-four hour average, so they are not the same quantity, and the dose-response relationship in the study is not linear. The readings this week are elevated. By how much the risk moves is not something the published work can tell you.
Where ultraviolet enters the picture

Particulate matter and ultraviolet radiation are different insults that converge on the same chemistry. The polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons carried on fine particles activate the aryl hydrocarbon receptor, a transcription factor expressed throughout the skin, which drives cytochrome P450 expression and generates reactive oxygen species5. Those species raise matrix metalloproteinase 1 and 3, which degrade collagen and elastin; they suppress collagen type 1 synthesis; and they reduce the structural proteins that hold the barrier together, including filaggrin, E-cadherin and the cytokeratins5. Ultraviolet A arrives at the same oxidative endpoint by a different route.

Whether the two are merely additive or worse in combination now has direct evidence. A 2025 study exposed primary human melanocytes and skin explants to ultraviolet, to urban particulate, and to both together for four consecutive days10. Only the combination reduced mitochondrial membrane potential and ATP beyond what either did alone, only the combination tipped cells from senescence into apoptosis, and the explants showed epidermal thinning and dermal melanin leakage resembling post-inflammatory hyperpigmentation10. About 30% of cells in the combined arm turned senescent.

The counterweight arrived the same year. A separate group exposed keratinocytes and human skin explants to benzo[a]pyrene, the model hydrocarbon, with and without ultraviolet11. In isolated keratinocytes the response was partially synergistic, as expected. In intact skin explants it was not: oxidative markers barely moved, DNA damage did not exceed ultraviolet alone, and the tissue demonstrated repair capacity the cell monolayers lacked11. Intact human skin defends itself considerably better than a dish of cells does. The synergy is real in the laboratory. How much of it survives in a living face is an open question, and the authors of the melanocyte study list the same caveat themselves: four days of controlled exposure in donor tissue from light-skinned neonates is not a proxy for Singaporean skin under Singaporean conditions10.
The thing most haze advice gets wrong

The intuitive assumption is that a sky full of smoke means less ultraviolet reaching the ground, and that photoprotection therefore matters less this week. The World Health Organization's guide to the solar ultraviolet index says the opposite in plain terms: scattering can increase total ultraviolet levels, and haze in the atmosphere can even increase ultraviolet exposure12. Over 90% of ultraviolet penetrates light cloud12. A dimmer, greyer sky is a poor guide to what reaches skin.

Nobody has measured this properly for Singapore. Thick absorbing smoke at high optical depth does reduce surface ultraviolet; lighter scattering haze can raise the diffuse component. Which effect dominates depends on the aerosol load, its composition and the sun's angle, and no published Singapore measurement resolves it for the conditions of this particular week. None of that supports a claim in either direction. The visual dimming of the sun is not evidence of anything, and treating it as permission to skip sunscreen is an inference resting on nothing.
What antioxidants have and have not shown

The most directly relevant trial is small and recent. Fifteen women with phototypes III and IV were exposed to 100 micrograms per cubic metre of particulate for two hours a day across four consecutive days, with three skin zones each: unexposed, exposed, and exposed after a topical antioxidant serum of ascorbic acid, ferulic acid and tocopherol13. In the exposed untreated zones, type I collagen fell by 30 to 40%, type III by around 60%, the oxidative marker 4-HNE rose by 61% and COX2 by 63%. The treated zones showed 43% less 4-HNE and 57% less COX2 than exposed skin, with filaggrin and involucrin substantially preserved13.

Those are striking numbers. Fifteen participants over four days is a pilot, every endpoint is a molecular marker read from a biopsy rather than a visible clinical outcome anyone would notice in a mirror, and several authors are employed by the cosmetics manufacturer whose formulation was tested13. The direction of the finding is plausible and mechanistically coherent. The magnitude, and whether it translates into anything a person can see, has not been established.

What this article is not claiming

Heliocare 360 D Plus is formulated around a standardised Polypodium leucotomos extract with niacinamide, vitamin D and vitamin E, and the manufacturer's published claims for it concern ultraviolet damage, oxidative neutralisation and photoageing14. No pollution or air quality claim is made for the product, and none is made here. Nothing in the published literature tests oral photoprotection against particulate exposure, so there is no evidence base on which such a claim could rest.

What the evidence supports doing

The gap between what has been demonstrated and what is being recommended online this week is wide. Almost nothing in the literature addresses a discrete haze episode directly. The recommendations below are drawn from what has been shown, with the reasoning attached, and they are deliberately unexciting.

• Keep the sunscreen exactly as it was. There is no measured basis for assuming ultraviolet has fallen, and the World Health Organization's own guidance points the other way12. Nothing about the haze makes a change to photoprotection rational.
  • Cleanse at the end of the day, and do not escalate it. Particles sit on the skin surface and in follicular openings5, so removing them is sensible. Aggressive cleansing is not: the same literature shows particulate exposure already degrades filaggrin and E-cadherin5, and stripping the barrier further works against you.
  • If you have eczema, treat this as a flare-risk week. This is the one recommendation with local, large-scale evidence behind it9. Keep to your maintenance routine rather than waiting for a flare to start.
  • An antioxidant step is reasonable, on modest expectations. The mechanism holds up and the pilot data point the right way, but the evidence is a fifteen-person industry-funded study reading biopsy markers13. Treat it as promising rather than proven.
  • Follow the agency's advisory for outdoor exertion rather than a skincare rule. The National Environment Agency publishes guidance by population group and updates it daily4. Reducing time outdoors is the only intervention here with a genuine evidence base behind it, and it happens to reduce both exposures at once.

The uncomfortable summary is that a haze week is a good reason to be consistent and a poor reason to buy anything new. The particulate load is doing something measurable to skin, the effect is modest at the exposures Singapore experiences, and the interventions with the strongest evidence behind them are the ones most people already own.

faq.q: Does haze make ultraviolet damage worse or better?
faq.a: Neither has been measured for Singapore under these conditions. The World Health Organization notes that atmospheric scattering can increase total ultraviolet levels and that haze can even increase exposure12, while dense absorbing smoke reduces surface ultraviolet. Because the answer depends on aerosol load, composition and sun angle, the practical response is to change nothing about photoprotection rather than to assume a direction.

faq.q: Should I stop wearing sunscreen during the haze?
faq.a: No. No measurement establishes that ultraviolet at ground level has fallen, and the visual dimming of the sky is not evidence that it has12. Separately, ultraviolet and particulate exposure converge on the same oxidative pathway5, so removing one of the two protections you have is the wrong direction.

faq.q: Will a week of haze age my skin?
faq.a: The published evidence does not answer that. The studies linking particulate exposure to pigment spots and skin ageing measure exposure accumulated over decades of urban living, in cohorts of 400 and 1,877 people78. Extrapolating from a lifetime of soot to one hazy fortnight is not something those studies support.

faq.q: Why does my eczema get worse when the haze comes?
faq.a: That association is the best-evidenced local effect. An analysis of 1,440,844 atopic dermatitis consultations at the National Skin Centre between 2009 and 2019 found a 10% higher consultation risk at the 90th percentile of PM2.5 compared with the median, with a confidence interval of 1.01 to 1.199. Particulate exposure also reduces barrier proteins including filaggrin and E-cadherin5, which is a plausible mechanism for the association.

faq.q: Does an oral supplement help against haze?
faq.a: No published study has tested oral photoprotection against particulate exposure. The manufacturer's claims for Heliocare 360 D Plus concern ultraviolet damage and photoageing, not pollution14, and this article makes no claim beyond that. The topical antioxidant evidence that does exist is a fifteen-person, four-day, industry-funded pilot reading biopsy markers rather than visible outcomes13.

blocks.html: The light your sunscreen was not built to filter

Sunlight is not one thing. It arrives as ultraviolet B, ultraviolet A, visible light including blue light, and infrared, and each one reaches a different depth in the skin. The SPF number on a bottle describes protection against ultraviolet B and, to a lesser degree, part of the ultraviolet A range. It says nothing about the rest of what is landing on you2.

That gap matters more here than the global advice suggests. Around half the sunlight reaching the ground is visible light, the part you can see, and in medium to deep skin tones it is the blue-violet end of that range which drives pigment2. A survey of 2,328 adults in Singapore found 53.4% with Fitzpatrick type III skin and another 19.1% type IV3, the medium-to-olive range on the six-point scale dermatologists use. Most of us, in other words, sit exactly where visible light does its work.

Outdoors that is the glare coming back off a pavement at one in the afternoon. Indoors it is the window seat on the bus home and the screen you spend the rest of the day in front of. None of it feels like sun exposure, and all of it reaches the cells that make pigment.

The words you will meet below

Pigment cell (melanocyte). The cell that manufactures melanin, sitting near the base of the outer skin layer rather than on the surface.

Surface skin cell (keratinocyte). The cells that make up most of the skin you can see. They receive finished pigment from the pigment cell and carry it upwards.

Tyrosinase. The enzyme that starts pigment production. Slow it down and less melanin gets made in the first place.

Renewal cycle. Skin replaces its outer layer roughly every twenty-eight days, which is the natural clock anything working at this depth runs on.
How a dark spot forms

Melanin is made in stages, and every stage is somewhere you can step in. Light and heat reach the skin and the surface cells respond by releasing chemical messengers. Those messengers reach the pigment cell, where tyrosinase switches on and converts a building-block amino acid into melanin through a short chain of steps. The finished pigment is packed into parcels, handed across to the surrounding surface cells, and carried up towards the top of the skin. Weeks later it shows on the cheek as a dark spot145.

Which is why a spot you notice this month started forming a while ago, and why anything working at the pigment cell is working on that same delay. The flipside is that stepping in early has more leverage than treating what has already surfaced.

Where each active steps in

Luminance places an active at four points along that chain rather than stacking four versions of the same idea. Fernblock and rosemary extract work at the top, on the oxidative stress and signalling that set the process going. Glutathione works inside the pigment cell, slowing tyrosinase by binding up the copper the enzyme needs to function4. Nicotinamide works at the hand-off, where finished pigment parcels move into the surface cells6.

Nicotinamide earns its place twice over. Beyond the pigment hand-off, it raises the skin's own production of ceramides and the other fats that make up the barrier holding moisture in7, which is why the formulation helps with dehydrated skin as well as uneven tone.
The dose, printed

Every capsule carries 240mg of Fernblock, together with 125mg of L-glutathione, 20mg of rosemary extract and 8mg of nicotinamide1. We recommend two capsules a day, one in the morning and one at night, which brings the daily Fernblock to 480mg.

Splitting the dose is deliberate rather than a convenience. Visible light and pollution exposure run right through the day instead of peaking at noon, so the cover is spread to match1. A pack holds sixty capsules, thirty days of two, sized to carry a full renewal cycle from start to finish1.

The fern has a useful backstory. Polypodium leucotomos started out as a water plant and adapted to life on land, evolving its own defences against ultraviolet radiation on the way1. Central American communities were using it for inflamed skin long before anyone standardised the extract1. Cantabria Labs has researched it for over twenty-five years, and it now carries more than fifty published laboratory and clinical studies1.
Why it is a capsule and not a cream

A cream works downwards from the surface, and the pigment cell sits below the level a topical comfortably reaches. Taking the actives orally sends them the other way. They arrive through the bloodstream and meet the pigment cell from underneath, which is the reason Luminance is a capsule1. It is designed to sit beneath a topical routine rather than compete with one.

Skin renews itself roughly every twenty-eight days, so the complexion you are looking at in a month is made of cells that were forming while you were taking it. Anything working this far upstream shows up on that clock rather than overnight.
What the research shows

The study worth knowing about is the one on visible light. Twenty-two people with medium to deep skin tones were exposed to a measured dose of visible light, about what 160 minutes outdoors delivers, then exposed again after twenty-eight days taking 480mg of the extract daily8. On instrument readings, two kinds of darkening came down significantly: the pigment that sets in soon after exposure, and the tan that deepens over the following days8.
The dose there is 480mg a day, exactly what two Luminance capsules deliver, and the period is twenty-eight days, exactly one pack.

Fernblock has been examined against ultraviolet too. In a separate study, twenty-two people took 240mg before ultraviolet B exposure and showed measurably less redness afterwards, alongside a higher threshold before their skin burned at all9.

Glutathione has its own supporting studies for skin tone close to ours. Thirty Filipino women of medium to deep skin tone taking a daily glutathione preparation showed a significant fall in melanin readings from where they started, with the change appearing in as little as two weeks10. A separate randomised, double-blind trial against placebo in fifty-seven women found significantly fewer wrinkles after twelve weeks11, and an earlier placebo-controlled study at a higher daily dose reported lower melanin readings than placebo across the same period12.
Rosemary adds antioxidant support that has been tested orally in people, in its case as part of a polyphenol combination13.
What changes beyond pigment

Cantabria Labs ran the finished formulation over twelve weeks in thirty-eight Asian women aged twenty-five to sixty, all with uneven complexion and visible signs of ageing, and all getting one to three hours of sun and pollution exposure daily14. Alongside the pigment work, the instruments recorded 10% more firmness and 17% more elasticity on a suction probe that measures how readily skin springs back, 19% less wrinkled area on a surface scanner, and 15% less water loss through the skin14. These figures come from the company's own study, held as data on file.

That last metric is the one people usually skip past, and it deserves a second look. Water loss through the skin is a barrier reading: the lower it runs, the better the skin is holding on to its own moisture. A barrier under less strain is also a barrier that reacts less, which is part of why dullness, uneven tone and dehydration so often turn up together.
Why people start using Heliocare Luminance

Most people come to it for uneven tone and dark spots built up over years of ordinary exposure. Others start alongside a clinic treatment aimed at pigment, where Luminance works as an adjuvant to whatever protocol the doctor has set rather than in place of it1. A third group starts ahead of an energy-based procedure, where the thinking is to have antioxidant cover established before the skin is challenged1.
How to take it

• Two capsules daily, split morning and night. That is 480mg of Fernblock a day, the dose used in the visible-light study8, spread across the hours you are exposed1.
  • Give it a full cycle. A pack is built around the twenty-eight day renewal cycle1, and the trials measuring pigment and firmness ran to twelve weeks1114.
  • Keep your sunscreen on. Every arm of the Luminance study wore sunscreen too14, and Luminance does not replace your regular Heliocare Oral1.
  • Suitable from sixteen. Halal certified, vegan friendly, and with no reported drug interactions, so it sits alongside other supplements. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should speak to a doctor first1.
  • Ask the clinic that knows your skin. Luminance is dispensed through dermatology, aesthetic and plastic surgery practices rather than retail1, so the conversation comes with someone qualified to have it.

Pigment is slow to arrive and slow to leave, and anything working at the pigment cell is working on that timescale rather than an overnight one. What Luminance offers is four actives placed along the pathway, at doses printed on the box, one of them matched exactly to the study behind it. It was tested alongside sunscreen, not instead of it.

faq.q: How long before I see a difference?
faq.a: One pack covers the twenty-eight day renewal cycle, which is the shortest sensible window to judge it on1. The visible-light study ran to twenty-eight days8, and the trials measuring pigment, firmness and wrinkles ran to twelve weeks1114. Pigment is slow to build and slow to fade, so give it a full cycle before deciding.

faq.q: Can I take it with Heliocare Oral?
faq.a: Yes, and you should. Luminance is formulated for pigment and visible signs of ageing rather than as a sun-protection capsule, so it sits alongside your regular Heliocare Oral rather than replacing it1.

faq.q: Why two capsules instead of one?
faq.a: Two capsules deliver 480mg of Fernblock daily, which is the dose used in the visible-light study8. Splitting them morning and night spreads the cover across the day, because visible light and pollution exposure do not stop after lunch1.

faq.q: Is it suitable for Asian skin?
faq.a: The research is closer to Asian skin than most. The visible-light study was run in medium to deep skin tones8, the glutathione work in Filipino women of similar tone10, and the Luminance formulation itself was studied in thirty-eight Asian women14.

faq.a: Luminance has no reported drug interactions, and it is halal certified, vegan friendly and suitable from age sixteen1. Pregnant and breastfeeding women should check with a doctor before starting any oral supplement1.
